results.name: lag1_response_repeat
results.description: Proportion of consecutive trials within a participant (by trial_index order) on which the yes/no answer repeats the previous answer; observed > null means sequential response perseveration (answer inertia) that the trial-independent model does not produce, observed < null means alternation.
results.code:
# name: lag1_response_repeat
# description: Proportion of consecutive trials within a participant (by trial_index order) on which the yes/no answer repeats the previous answer; observed > null means sequential response perseveration (answer inertia) that the trial-independent model does not produce, observed < null means alternation.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].to_numpy() == 0).cumsum()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(int)
    same_p = pid[1:] == pid[:-1]
    rep = (r[1:] == r[:-1])[same_p]
    return float(rep.mean())

results.name: target_in_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples; observed < null means people sometimes reject an already-shown example (lapses/random responding) that the lapse-free model, predicting near-certain yes, does not produce.

results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on the second half of each participant's session (trial_index >= 225) minus the first half; a nonzero observed value against a null near 0 means responding drifts over the session (fatigue/criterion shift), which the stationary model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on the second half of each participant's session (trial_index >= 225) minus the first half; a nonzero observed value against a null near 0 means responding drifts over the session (fatigue/criterion shift), which the stationary model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    late = ti >= 225
    return float(r[late].mean() - r[~late].mean())

results.name: single_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials with a single example whose target differs from it; observed > null means people generalise more broadly from one example than the model's size-principle learner predicts (observed < null: more conservatively).
results.code:
# name: single_example_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on trials with a single example whose target differs from it; observed > null means people generalise more broadly from one example than the model's size-principle learner predicts (observed < null: more conservatively).
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ok = (n == 1) & (E[:, 0] != t)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if ok.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[ok].mean())

results.name: recency_last_vs_first_example
results.description: Among multi-example sets and targets not in the set, yes rate when the target is closer to the last-shown example than to the first-shown example minus yes rate when it is closer to the first; observed > null (null ~0, model is order-invariant) means a recency effect in generalisation, observed < null a primacy effect.
results.code:
# name: recency_last_vs_first_example
# description: Among multi-example sets and targets not in the set, yes rate when the target is closer to the last-shown example than to the first-shown example minus yes rate when it is closer to the first; observed > null (null ~0, model is order-invariant) means a recency effect in generalisation, observed < null a primacy effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    first = E[:, 0]
    last = E[np.arange(len(E)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    ok = (n >= 2) & ~in_set
    df1 = np.abs(t - first); dl = np.abs(t - last)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = ok & (dl < df1); b = ok & (df1 < dl)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: parity_congruence_within_span
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples all of one parity, among targets inside [min,max] of the examples and not in the set, yes rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null means people use parity within the magnitude range more strongly than the model (which only gets parity through whole-range odd/even rules) predicts.
results.code:
# name: parity_congruence_within_span
# description: For sets of >=2 examples all of one parity, among targets inside [min,max] of the examples and not in the set, yes rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null means people use parity within the magnitude range more strongly than the model (which only gets parity through whole-range odd/even rules) predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    par = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, E % 2)
    pmin = np.nanmin(par, axis=1); pmax = np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    ok = (n >= 2) & (pmin == pmax) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~in_set
    same = (t % 2) == pmin
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = ok & same; b = ok & ~same
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: near_vs_far_outside_span
results.description: Among targets outside [min,max] of a multi-example set, yes rate for targets 1-10 away from the nearest edge minus yes rate for targets more than 25 away; observed > null means human generalisation falls off with distance beyond the examples more steeply than the model's interval hypotheses produce (observed < null: flatter).
results.code:
# name: near_vs_far_outside_span
# description: Among targets outside [min,max] of a multi-example set, yes rate for targets 1-10 away from the nearest edge minus yes rate for targets more than 25 away; observed > null means human generalisation falls off with distance beyond the examples more steeply than the model's interval hypotheses produce (observed < null: flatter).
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dist = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0.0))
    ok = n >= 2
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = ok & (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 10); b = ok & (dist > 25)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: participant_yes_rate_sd
results.description: SD across participants (rows in blocks; a new participant starts whenever trial_index == 0) of the overall yes rate; observed > null means people differ in their yes-bias / generalisation breadth more than the single shared-parameter model produces.
results.code:
# name: participant_yes_rate_sd
# description: SD across participants (rows in blocks; a new participant starts whenever trial_index == 0) of the overall yes rate; observed > null means people differ in their yes-bias / generalisation breadth more than the single shared-parameter model produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].to_numpy() == 0).cumsum()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    rates = pd.Series(r).groupby(pid).mean()
    return float(rates.std(ddof=0))
